verses.translation_literal: Of David, in his changing his taste before Abimelech, and he drove him away, and he went.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song of David, from the day he put on another face before Abimelech: the king drove him out, and he walked away alive.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the superscription, and in the Hebrew it counts as verse 1, which is why the KJV numbers everything after it one lower and leaves this line as 34:0. It sets the scene for an acrostic poem of thanks. The story is 1 Samuel 21:11-16. David has run from Saul to Gath, the city of Goliath, and the king's servants recognize him as the man the women sang about. Frightened, David scratches at the gate doors and lets spittle run down his beard, and Achish sends him away, asking whether he is short of madmen. Abimelech is not a slip. Rashi, Radak and Meiri all say it was a title of Philistine kings, as 'Pharaoh' was for Egypt's, and that Achish was his own name.

The KJV has 'changed his behaviour', which hides the Hebrew. The word is ṭaʿam, literally 'taste', and the same root drives 'taste and see' in verse 9. The poem begins with a man making himself taste wrong to his enemies and ends up asking his hearers to taste the LORD. The last three verbs are short and flat: he drove him away, and he went. No speech, no triumph, only a man leaving a court he should not have left alive.

philological_notes.note: 'Taste', and so judgment, discernment, a stated decision (as in Jonah 3:7, the king's decree). Here it is the outward manner David changed: his speech and conduct, as the Philistines saw it. The same root is the command 'taste' in verse 9.
A royal title borne by Philistine kings of Gerar in Genesis 20 and 26, here the king of Gath who is called Achish in 1 Samuel 21.

verses.translation_literal: I will bless [obj] YHWH at every time, continually his praise [is] in my mouth.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will bless the LORD at every hour. His praise will not leave my mouth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first line of the acrostic begins with aleph, and the poem is written for memory: a song a man can recite in a cave or on the road. The singer sets no occasion. 'At every time' means in good hours and bad ones. Ibn Ezra says it includes the hour of his feigned madness, and Malbim says the bad times are blessed because they serve a good end. For David, hungry and hunted at Gath, this is a stubborn vow, not a mood.

The KJV 'shall continually be in my mouth' turns a verbless Hebrew clause into a future. The Hebrew has 'his praise in my mouth' with no verb, as a plain fact. 'Mouth' is a body word, and praise here is something spoken aloud, not a feeling.

philological_notes.note: The cohortative: 'let me bless, I will bless', a resolve said aloud. The root also means 'knee' (to kneel); to bless God is to acknowledge him as the source of good.

verses.translation_literal: In YHWH will boast my self; let the humble hear and let them rejoice.
verses.translation_dramatic: My whole self boasts, and its boast is the LORD. Let the humble hear it, and be glad.
verses.directors_commentary:
Bet, the second letter. The verb is hitpael of hll, from the same root as 'Hallelujah', and it means to boast or glory in something, not merely to praise. A man who a moment ago slobbered into his beard now brags, and what he brags about is not himself. Rashi puts it as 'I boast that I have such a patron to rescue and protect me'. The word 'patron' lands harder for an ancient reader than for us, since a client in the Near East depended on a protector for his food and his life.

The KJV 'make her boast' adds a pronoun the verb does not have, and 'meek' (ASV) blurs ʿănavim, the humble or bowed, those with nothing to boast of. The wish is jussive: let them hear. They are the audience he wants: the poor, not the powerful.

philological_notes.note: Reflexive: 'praise oneself, boast'. It carries the sense of loud, public glorying. Rashi glosses it with the Old French porvantra, 'to vaunt'.
'The humble, the bowed down'. Close in sound and sense to ʿani, 'poor', in verse 7. Radak says only these, not the proud who hated David, will rejoice.

verses.translation_literal: Make great to YHWH with me, and let us exalt his name together.
verses.translation_dramatic: Come, make the LORD great with me. Together let us lift his name on high.
verses.directors_commentary:
Gimel. The singer turns from his own voice to a chorus. 'With me' matters: he does not ask them to praise on his behalf, he asks them to join. 'Together' closes the verse so that no one sings alone.

Two verbs do different work. To 'make great' is to say how large he is, and to 'exalt' is to lift him up. Malbim reads the pair as a contrast: the nations made God lofty and out of reach, Israel makes him great and near. The KJV 'magnify' is good English but suggests a lens. The Hebrew is the plain causative of 'be big'.

philological_notes.note: Piel imperative of 'be great': 'declare him great, make him great'. It is an act of recognition, not a change in God.

verses.translation_literal: I sought [obj] YHWH and he answered me, and from all my fears he delivered me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I went looking for the LORD, and he answered me. Out of every fear that held me, he pulled me free.
verses.directors_commentary:
Dalet. This is the testimony that backs the vow. The verb dārash is more than 'ask': it is to seek out, to enquire, the word used for going to a prophet or a sanctuary. Radak thinks David did it silently in his heart, standing among the Philistines with no altar and no priest. Whatever the setting, the order is plain: sought, answered, delivered.

The KJV 'heard me' softens ʿānāni. To answer is more than to listen, since an answer is a reply. The object is 'fears', mĕgurot, a rare word for dreads from the root gur, 'to be afraid' (Rashi compares Numbers 22:3). The KJV's 'fears' is fine, but the plural is the point: not one danger, all of them.

philological_notes.note: 'My dreads', a rare noun. Rashi ties it to wayyagor in Numbers 22:3 ('Moab was in dread') and Metzudat Zion glosses it simply 'my fears'. BDB derives it from gur, 'to be afraid'.

verses.translation_literal: They looked to him and they shone, and their faces, let them not be ashamed.
verses.translation_dramatic: They turned their eyes toward him, and light came into them; they brightened like a morning after a long night. And their faces, lifted and open, will never burn with shame.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker steps from his own story (verses 5 and 7) to a crowd: the plural "they" are anyone who looks to the LORD out of trouble (Rashi on Psalms 34:6: "all those who looked to him from the midst of their distress"). The scene is the face. In the ancient Near East shame was something worn on the face, a flush, a dropped gaze, a face turned down before the creditor or the judge. The poem pairs the two faces: one that glows, one that does not go pale or hot with disgrace. Radak (on Psalms 34:6) notes exactly this: shame shows in the face.

The KJV "were lightened" is archaic and ambiguous; to modern ears it sounds like a burden taken off, but nahar here is about light, as in Job 3:4 (נהרה, "radiance"), and so "they shone" or "were radiant" (ASV). There is an older alternative, mentioned by Ibn Ezra and Radak, that nahar means "to flow" (as in Jer 31:12, "they shall flow to the goodness of the LORD"): then the verse reads "they looked to him and streamed toward him." Light and flow may both sound in the ear. The last clause the KJV turns into a plain past, "were not ashamed". The Hebrew uses ʾal with the imperfect, the form of a wish or a firm promise: "let their faces not be shamed." That is a guarantee spoken over the audience, not a report.

philological_notes.note: Most commentators read it as "be radiant, shine" (the root of נְהָרָה, Job 3:4, cited by Metzudat Zion and Radak). Radak also records the sense "flow, run" (Jer 31:12; Isa 2:2), which would make the verse a movement toward God, not only a brightening of the face.

"Be ashamed, be abashed." This is the חפר of shame, not the חפר "to dig". Rashi compares Isa 24:23, "the moon shall be confounded and the sun ashamed" (וְחָפְרָה הַלְּבָנָה). Paired with אל it is a jussive: a wish or promise.

verses.translation_literal: This poor one called out, and YHWH heard, and from all his troubles he saved him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Here is one poor man. He cried out, and the LORD heard him. From every trouble he had, he was saved.
verses.directors_commentary:
Zayin. The pointing finger of 'this' is the sound in the room. Radak and Meiri say David means himself. Malbim hears the faces of verse 6 speaking: 'look, this poor man called, and the LORD heard'. Either way an actor should point, and the sentence should sound like evidence put before a court.

The poor man, ʿani, is one of the many words for people with no protector: no land, no family, no patron. The KJV 'poor man' is correct, but 'man' is not in the Hebrew. Ibn Ezra notes that 'heard' is a perfect even though it sits after a pause, as the grammar of the line allows. The final verb, hoshiʿo, is the root of 'Joshua' and 'Jesus', to bring into open space: to save is to give room. 'From all his troubles' repeats 'from all my fears' of verse 5, so the pattern of verses 5 and 7 mirrors itself.

philological_notes.note: 'Poor, afflicted, bowed down'. Sounds like ʿănavim of verse 3 and the 'answered' of verse 5, ʿānāni, all from the same consonants ʿ-n.
'He saved him', literally 'he brought him into a broad place'. The same root gives the name Joshua.

verses.translation_literal: Encamping, the angel of YHWH, around those who fear him, and he rescues them.
verses.translation_dramatic: The angel of the LORD pitches his tent in a ring around those who fear him, and he pulls them out of danger.
verses.directors_commentary:
Chet. The picture is a military one. The verb ḥoneh means to pitch camp, and the image is an army bivouacked in a circle around a small group, which is how a besieging force surrounds a town, turned inside out. Radak says it directly: when enemies camp round about them to do harm, the angel of the LORD camps round about them, and the enemies cannot touch them. Ibn Ezra adds that 'angel' may stand for the whole kind, as in 'I have ox and ass': many angels, as with Elisha at Dothan.

The KJV 'encampeth round about' is correct but old. The Hebrew line is a participle, 'encamping', with no stated subject first: the word order puts the verb in front of the angel, so the audience hears the tents going up before they know whose. The last verb, 'and he rescues them', is from ḥālaṣ, to draw out or pull free, with a nuance of arming for battle (the YLT 'armeth them', Malbim's 'makes them armed').

philological_notes.note: A participle of 'pitch camp': an ongoing, present act. It is the military verb of Exodus 14:2 and Judges 6:4.
'And he rescues them', from ḥālaṣ 'draw out, pull free'. The same root names an armed man (ḥālūṣ), so the sense of 'arming' (YLT) is also present; I give 'rescues' as the main sense.

verses.translation_literal: Taste and see that YHWH [is] good; how blessed [is] the man [who] takes refuge in him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Taste it. See it for yourselves: the LORD is good. Happy the man who runs to him for shelter.
verses.directors_commentary:
Tet, and the most quoted verse of the psalm. Two senses are named in one breath: the tongue and the eye. Ibn Ezra says 'taste' is the sight of the heart and 'see' the sight of the eye. Radak and Meiri read 'taste' as a figure for judgment by testing, the way you taste food to learn whether it is bitter or sweet, and cite Proverbs 31:18, 'she tastes that her merchandise is good'. Malbim notes that human help can be sweet or useful, but this help is good as well.

The verb is the same ṭaʿam of verse 1. David changed his 'taste' before a king in order to survive, and now he commands the poor to taste the LORD. The KJV 'O taste and see' softens a command in the plural to an invitation. 'Trusteth' for yeḥĕseh weakens the image: ḥāsāh means to take refuge, to run under cover, as a bird under wings or a man into a cave. The word is physical. The man in 'blessed is the man' is gever, the strong one, not ʾādām.

philological_notes.note: 'Taste', figurative for test by experience. The same root as ṭaʿam in verse 1 and the Hebrew 'to taste' in Proverbs 31:18.
'Takes refuge'. The image is shelter, not an inner attitude: a place to hide from danger.
'The man' as a strong or able person, here set beside the poor man of verse 7: even the strong man has to take refuge.

verses.translation_literal: Fear [obj] YHWH, his holy ones, for [there is] no lack to those who fear him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Fear the LORD, you who are his own, set apart for him. Those who fear him lack nothing.
verses.directors_commentary:
Yod. The command is addressed to qĕdoshav, 'his holy ones', meaning those set apart for him. 'Saints' in the KJV has Christian overtones that came later; in the Hebrew it is closer to 'his consecrated people'. Radak links it to the nazirite, who is 'holy to the LORD' (Numbers 6:8), and reads: you who content yourselves with little, do not fear that your food will run short. Malbim sets them against the ascetics of the nations, who withdrew from the world and went short, while the LORD's holy ones are not asked to deny themselves.

Two senses of 'fear' are in play. The first is yĕruʾ, a command, and Ibn Ezra and Radak note that its aleph is silent, to keep it from being confused with yirʾu, 'they see'. The second is yĕreʾav, 'those who fear him', a noun phrase. The KJV 'no want' loses the physical word maḥsor, an empty storehouse. The audience is a runaway with no household and no land, in the country of an enemy; Radak says no one there knew him enough to give him bread, and for him this was a claim about food.

philological_notes.note: 'His holy ones', the set-apart. Radak ties it to the nazirite of Numbers 6:8; Malbim sets it against pagan ascetics.
'Lack, want': an empty store. It is the noun of the verb yaḥsĕru in verse 11.

verses.translation_literal: Young lions are in want and they are hungry, and the seekers of YHWH, they will not lack any good.
verses.translation_dramatic: Even the young lions, the strong ones, go thin with want, and their bellies cry out for food. But those who seek the LORD will not be left without a single good thing.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a proverb built on a contrast of two appetites. The kefirim, young lions in their prime, were the Bible's image of strength and successful hunting; a lion that cannot find prey is a picture of strength failing (Radak on Psalms 34:11 quotes Job 4:11, "the lion perishes for lack of prey"). Rashi on this verse notes that kol tov is idiomatic: with a negative it means "any" (like kol melakha, Ex 12:16), so "they shall not lack any good thing." The two verbs for the lions, rashu and raʿevu, are a pair: "they are impoverished" and "they are hungry." Metzudat Zion links rashu to the word rash, "a poor man" (the Hebrew calls it "from the language of rash and ʿani"), so the strong one is brought down to the poor man's lot, close in sense to the ʿani of verse 7, though not from the same root.

The KJV "do lack, and suffer hunger" lets "suffer" hide the second verb, a plain "are hungry". It also turns the second half, "they that seek the LORD", into a future with "shall", where the Hebrew uses the imperfect lo yachseru, a general truth ("do not lack"). Commentators read the lions figuratively. Ibn Ezra says: men like lions in their gorging; Metzudat David: the great and the rich; Meiri: those who live by taking. Ibn Ezra also records an old view that the word means "deniers" (kofrim), a pun on kefirim; I keep the literal beast, since the bite of the proverb is the strong animal made hungry. The Targum has "those who seek the teaching of the LORD", an interpretive addition: the Hebrew has only "seekers of YHWH". To "seek" (darash) is the verb for turning to God for guidance, so the verse sets the reliance of the pious against the self-reliance of the powerful.

philological_notes.note: "Young lions", lions old enough to hunt for themselves; a standard image of power and of the violent. The commentators in the packet read it as a figure for rich or rapacious men (Metzudat David, Ibn Ezra, Meiri).

"Be poor, be in want." Rashi glosses "the language of poverty" (דלות); Metzudat Zion connects it with the word rash, "a poor man". It is the root of the participle רָשׁ, "poor", not ענה (the root of ʿani in verse 7).
"Those who seek YHWH": to inquire of him, to turn to him for help or guidance. It is set against the lions, who seek their own prey.

verses.translation_literal: Come, children, listen to me; the fear of YHWH I will teach you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Come, children. Listen to me, and I will teach you what it is to fear the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
Lamed, the Hebrew letter whose name means 'to teach', and the verse opens the second half of the psalm, which turns from thanks to instruction. The voice changes from a man in danger to a teacher with an audience at his knee. The speaker is now a sage, using the language of wisdom, as in Proverbs, where 'my son' begins a lesson.

Two things the KJV hides. 'Come' is lĕkhu, literally 'go', the verb of motion that Radak says is a call to action and not a command to walk, as in Isaiah 1:18, 'Come now, let us reason together'. Metzudat Zion makes the same point with Genesis 37:20. And 'children' is banim, 'sons', which Radak says means those who listen and keep the teacher's lesson, as 'sons of the prophets' means disciples. Malbim reads it more broadly: unlike the pagan priesthoods, the fear of the LORD is open to children, not kept for the great and the priestly. The fear he promises to teach is a trained habit, one that can be learned, and the next verses show what it looks like in speech and conduct.

philological_notes.note: 'Go', used as a spur to action, 'come on', rather than movement from a place.
'Sons, children'; in a teaching setting, disciples. Radak compares 'sons of the prophets'.
'I will teach you', piel of lmd; the same root as the 'ox goad' (malmad), a prod that trains.

verses.translation_literal: Who [is] the man, the one desiring life, loving days, to see good?
verses.translation_dramatic: Who is the man here who wants life? Who loves the days given him, and longs to look upon good?
verses.directors_commentary:
The teacher turns from his own thanksgiving to the listeners and asks a question like a street-seller calling out his wares. The speaker is not asking for volunteers from a few pious people; he is asking everyone, because everyone wants it. Play it warm and a little playful, then wait for the room to answer by its silence.

The KJV 'What man is he' is archaic and its added 'many' and 'that he may see' flatten the grammar. The Hebrew is blunt: a participle phrase ('the one desiring life'), a second ('loving days'), then an infinitive: 'to see good'. 'Days' means a full measure of days, a long life, and 'to see' good means to experience it, as in 'see death' or 'see trouble'. In a world without antibiotics or a safety net, a long life and a good one was the whole definition of blessing. Radak and Meiri hear here also the life of the world to come; Malbim reads it against the ascetics of the nations who despise life, so that the teacher offers a faith that does not flee the world.

philological_notes.note: The participle with the article means 'the one who delights in, wants'. It names a settled desire, not a passing wish. The same root appears for God's delight in the Psalms.
'To see good' means to experience good, not merely to watch it. Metzudat David takes it as true good in the world to come; the plain sense is a life that is lived well.

verses.translation_literal: Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then guard your tongue from evil. Guard your lips, so that no deceit is spoken through them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer is not a ritual or a pilgrimage. It begins with speech. The teacher speaks in the singular, 'you', as to each person in the crowd. Keep the voice quiet and steady, like a man laying a hand on a shoulder.

The verb nitzor is the one used for a watchman guarding a city or a vineyard: the tongue is a gate that has to be manned. 'Evil' (ra') is broad: slander, false witness, curses. 'Deceit' (mirmah) is more specific, the word for fraud and trickery, and Radak explains it as saying one thing with the mouth and holding another in the heart. KJV 'guile' is archaic; modern readers hear 'deceit' or 'fraud'. In a village economy where one's word sealed a sale or an oath, this was a civic and economic rule as much as a moral one. Malbim ties the verse to Doeg's report against the priests of Nob.

philological_notes.note: To keep, watch, guard; the watchman's verb (a besieged city, a vineyard). The tongue is treated as a gate that needs a guard.
Deceit, fraud, treachery. Radak glosses it as saying one thing with the mouth and another in the heart, and cites Jeremiah 9:7.

verses.translation_literal: Turn aside from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.
verses.translation_dramatic: Turn away from evil. Do good. Seek peace, and when it slips from you, run after it.
verses.directors_commentary:
Four short commands, two pairs, hammered one after another. Let the rhythm march: a turning away, a doing, a seeking, a chasing. The first pair says what to leave and what to put in its place, and Ibn Ezra reads them as the prohibitions and the commands of the law. The second pair raises the pitch.

Shalom is not just the absence of war. It is wholeness, a state of things being right between people. The verbs matter: 'seek' (baqesh) is what you do for something lost, and 'pursue' (radaf) is what a hunter or soldier does to a fleeing target. The KJV 'depart' and 'seek and pursue' keep this well; BBE's 'desiring it with all your heart' loses the chase. Peace does not come to you; it has to be run down. Rashi reads the two verbs by place, seek it where you are, pursue it elsewhere, and cites Tanhuma on Numbers.

philological_notes.note: 'Pursue it': the verb of a hunter or of an army chasing a fleeing enemy. Here it is turned from violence to peace. Rashi takes 'seek' for peace in one's own place and 'pursue' for peace elsewhere.

verses.translation_literal: [The] eyes of YHWH [are] toward [the] righteous, and his ears toward their cry for help.
verses.translation_dramatic: The eyes of the LORD are turned toward the righteous, and his ears bend toward their cry.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker now gives the reason for the commands: someone is watching, and he is on the side of those who live this way. The sentence has no verb, only two bare prepositional phrases, so it reads like a statement of fact, not a promise. Keep it simple and unhurried.

Body-language for God (eyes, ears, then face in the next verse) is how the ancient poet makes divine attention concrete. Ibn Ezra says eyes and ears stand for what is hidden and what is spoken. The KJV adds 'upon' and 'are open unto', which makes it a little more passive than the Hebrew; the Hebrew only says 'to', toward. Shav'ah is a cry for help, a loud shout from someone in danger, not a quiet prayer. The righteous (tzaddiqim) are those who stand in the right in their community, not those who are flawless.

philological_notes.note: A cry for help from someone in distress, louder than ordinary prayer. Malbim notes that sometimes they cry out over a harm that only seems so to them, and God still answers.

verses.translation_literal: [The] face of YHWH [is] against doers of evil, to cut off their memory from [the] earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the face of the LORD is set against those who do evil, to cut their memory from the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The warmth of the last verse turns on a single word: 'face'. Drop the voice. The same God who looks with eyes at the righteous now turns his face, and a turned face is a hard one. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read 'face' as anger that shows on the face, and Rashi compares Leviticus 20:5, 'I will set my face against that man'.

The punishment is not only death but erasure. 'Memory' (zeker) is the name by which a person is remembered, the standing of his family after him. In a culture where a man lived on in his name and his descendants, to cut that off was worse than a quick death. KJV 'remembrance' is fine; the Hebrew verb 'cut off' (lehakhrit) is the same one used for cutting a covenant, so it carries the sound of a sentence handed down. YLT places the verse in brackets because it reads like an aside before the cry of the next verse.

philological_notes.note: 'Face of'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion take it here as the face of anger, since anger is seen in the face, and cite Leviticus 20:3 and 20:5.
'Their memory': the name and remembrance that outlive a person. To cut it off is to remove the family from the community's memory.

verses.translation_literal: They cried out, and YHWH heard, and from all their troubles he delivered them.
verses.translation_dramatic: They cried out, and the LORD heard. Out of every trouble that pressed on them, he drew them free.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poem goes back to the cry of verse 16, and the pace picks up: three short clauses, a cry, a hearing, a rescue. Play the middle clause with a beat of stillness, 'and the LORD heard', since the whole Psalm began with a man who once cried and was heard.

The Hebrew gives no subject for 'they cried'. KJV and ASV insert 'the righteous', following Rashi and Radak, who say the verse returns to the righteous even though the verse about evildoers comes between; Meiri compares Deuteronomy 15:17. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David instead allow a reading about the wicked who turn back and cry. BBE turns the clause into 'the cry of the upright comes before the Lord', which is a paraphrase. The Hebrew also leaves 'troubles' as 'tzarot', the same root as 'narrow, tight': being pinned in a narrow place, which is exactly what rescue (hitzil, to pull out) undoes.

philological_notes.note: 'Their troubles', from the root for narrowness, tightness: a tight place. The deliverer then 'pulls out' (hitzil) from the tight place.
To pull out, snatch away, rescue. Often used of taking someone out of the hand of an enemy.

verses.translation_literal: Near [is] YHWH to the broken of heart, and [obj] the crushed of spirit he saves.
verses.translation_dramatic: Near, the LORD is near. Not to the proud, not to the strong. He is near to those whose hearts have been broken in pieces, and those whose spirit has been ground down to dust: these he lifts out, and these he saves.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the first time the psalm uses the word qarov, 'near', and it says who the nearness is for: the shattered. Earlier the psalm told of crying out and being heard; here God's presence is promised, and it is promised to people at their lowest, not to the successful. Play the line quietly, with no triumph in it.

The verse has two halves of one thought, two kinds of breaking: nishberei lev, 'broken of heart', and dakke'ei ruach, 'crushed of spirit'. Radak calls the second a repetition of the first in other words, and Metzudat Zion glosses dakka as 'crushed and broken'. Readers split on who is meant. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David take the broken-hearted as those who have turned back from their evil ways, the penitent; Radak and Malbim take them as those suffering under trouble. The Hebrew names no cause, so keep the line open to both. In Hebrew, 'heart' is the seat of will and thought, not of sentiment, and 'spirit' (ruach) is breath and inner force; to be crushed in spirit is to have no breath left to stand on.

KJV 'of a broken heart' and 'of a contrite spirit' rewrite the Hebrew into singular nouns with tidy adjectives. The Hebrew has plural participles, 'the broken ones' and 'the crushed ones': a group of people, not one state of mind. 'Contrite' also pushes the reading toward repentance, which the Hebrew word dakka does not say; it says 'crushed'. The object marker before the second phrase (ve'et) puts the crushed first in the clause and leaves the verb for last: 'the crushed of spirit, he saves.'

philological_notes.note: Plural niphal participle in the construct, 'those broken of heart'. The verb shavar is the one used in v.21 of bones that are not broken, so the verse and v.21 sit on the same root: the body is kept whole, the heart is broken and still met. Ibn Ezra reads these as the penitent.
'Crushed of spirit'. Dakka is rare in Hebrew; Metzudat Zion glosses it 'crushing and breaking', and Radak reads the second half of the verse as a restatement of the first.

verses.translation_literal: Many [are] the evils of [the] righteous one, and from all of them YHWH delivers him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Many are the evils that fall on the righteous. And out of every one of them, the LORD brings him free.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the teacher is honest with his listeners: the righteous do suffer. He does not promise a life without trouble. Say the first half plainly, then let the second half rise from it, so the faith is heard to cost something.

The word 'evils' (ra'ot) is the same word as the 'evil' the listener was told to turn from in verse 15; it covers moral evil and plain misfortune, so what the righteous man has to bear is the same stuff as what he is told to avoid. KJV 'afflictions' picks one sense. The line works by contrast of number: 'many' against 'all of them', and the 'righteous' is singular, one person, while the troubles are plural. Rashi says many evils and terrors come upon him and he is saved from all. Radak, citing Proverbs 24:16, says the righteous may fall seven times and rise; the deliverance is not that he is never struck but that he does not stay down.

philological_notes.note: 'Evils, troubles', plural of ra'ah. The same root as ra' in verses 14 and 15: the word covers wrongdoing and hardship alike, so context decides, and here it is hardship.

verses.translation_literal: Keeping all his bones, one from them not was broken.
verses.translation_dramatic: He keeps watch over every bone in the body of the one who is his. Count them, if you can. Not one of them has been broken.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is a sentence of bookkeeping: all, and then one, and then not. 'Keeping' is the same verb, shamar, that watches a flock or guards a city gate; here the guard is on the skeleton, the frame that holds a body up. Ibn Ezra says the bones are named because they are the foundations of the body, and Meiri and Radak agree. A broken bone in the ancient world was often the end of a man who had to walk or fight or work; to keep every bone is to keep the man standing. Say it as a quiet count, not a boast.

The Hebrew also carries a small grammar surprise. 'Bones' (ʿatzamot) is grammatically feminine in Hebrew, so 'one' (achat) and the verb 'was broken' (nishbarah) are feminine, and the spoken line has a rhythm of repeated -ah and -ot sounds. Radak points out something that is easy to lose in print: the stress in nishbarah falls on the next-to-last syllable (milʿel), which makes it a past-tense niphal, 'was broken' (an event), whereas the same spelling in Psalm 51:19, ruach nishbarah, is stressed on the last syllable (milraʿ) and is a stative, 'a broken spirit' (a state). So the form means 'was broken, once, as an event', not 'is a broken thing'.

KJV 'He keepeth all his bones: not one of them is broken' is close. Its 'is broken' reads as a present state, where the Hebrew says that the event has not happened. KJV also hides that the 'he' is the righteous person of the previous verse, while the keeper is YHWH, who is not named in this line. The reader must carry him over from v.20.

philological_notes.note: Niphal perfect, third feminine singular, stressed on the next-to-last syllable (milʿel), so an event: 'was broken'. Radak contrasts Psalm 51:19, ruach nishbarah, where the stress is on the last syllable (milraʿ) and the form is a stative: 'a broken spirit'.
Participle, 'keeping', a continuing watch, not a single act. The subject is YHWH of v.20, who is not named here. Rashi supplies it: 'the Holy One, blessed be he'.

verses.translation_literal: Evil will kill [the] wicked, and [the] haters of [the] righteous will be held guilty.
verses.translation_dramatic: But for the wicked, evil itself is the killer. And those who hate the righteous will be held guilty.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Psalm turns to the other side, and the tone hardens. Where the righteous had many troubles and was rescued from all, the wicked has one, and it kills. Ibn Ezra sees this counterweight to 'many evils' in verse 20: one evil is enough.

The word 'ra'ah' is the same word again, so the wicked is undone by the thing he does; the line has the irony of a trap closing on the one who set it. Radak cites Psalm 7:16, the pit that one digs and falls into; Metzudat David says the sin itself accuses him. The grammar is a little strange: 'evil' is the subject and it 'will kill' (the intensive form of the verb), so the sense is that it puts him to death for good. The last verb, ye'shamu, the KJV renders 'shall be desolate' and the ASV 'condemned'; the Hebrew root is asham, 'bear guilt', and the same verb returns in the next verse for the opposite fate. Radak and Metzudat Zion link it instead to 'desolation' (shamem), so the translators split.

philological_notes.note: A causative intensive: 'will bring to death', 'will kill off'. The subject is ra'ah, 'evil', which acts on the wicked as if it had its own hand. Rashi reads the evil as the harm the wicked himself does.

'They will bear guilt' or 'be held guilty'. Radak and Metzudat Zion connect it to shamem, 'be desolate' (Hosea 14:1, Joel 1:18), which gives KJV 'desolate'. The verb returns in the next verse in the negative.

verses.translation_literal: Redeeming, YHWH, the life of his servants, and not will be held guilty all the taking-refuge in him.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD buys back the lives of his servants. And not one who has run to him for shelter will be held guilty. Not one.
verses.directors_commentary:
The acrostic has ended and then does one more thing. The alphabet runs aleph to tav, and v.22 closes it on tav. This verse is an extra line that starts with pe, a letter the poem already used at v.17 (penei YHWH, 'the face of YHWH'). Play it as an afterword: the formal poem is over, and the speaker adds the last line by hand.

The verse opens with the participle 'redeeming' and puts YHWH second in the clause. The English order 'The LORD redeems' loses that. Padah is the verb of buying back, of ransom or of releasing a person from a debt, and it is said of the firstborn son and of slaves. Here the thing redeemed is nefesh, 'life' or 'throat', the whole living person; Radak reads it as the lives that the wicked plan to take.

The last clause plays on v.22. There, 'those who hate the righteous' ye'shamu, 'will be held guilty'. Here, 'all who take refuge in him' lo ye'shamu, 'will not be held guilty'. The same verb, with one negative in front, closes the poem on a mirror. KJV 'desolate' for both hides the repetition by using the sense of 'laid waste' (from shamam), which Radak and Ibn Ezra defend; but Rashi hears guilt and regret ('they will not regret that they took refuge in you'), as do ASV 'condemned' and the Hebrew's usual sense of asham, 'guilt, liability'. 'Take refuge' (chasah) is a concrete picture, of a bird under a wing or a traveller in a rock shelter, and KJV 'trust' turns it into an inner attitude.

philological_notes.note: Participle of padah, 'to redeem, to buy back', used of ransoming a firstborn or a slave or a life from death. As a participle it names what YHWH is doing, not one past act.

'Will be held guilty'. The vocalization here, with a sheva under the aleph and the shin, differs from the form in v.22; Radak remarks on the sheva pattern. Radak, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion link the verb to shamam, 'be desolate' (as in Hosea 14:1, Joel 1:18), which is where KJV 'desolate' comes from; Rashi reads it as regret or guilt.

'Those who take refuge in him', a participle: people who are sheltering now. Chasah is used of a bird's shelter beneath wings and of shelter in a rock; trust is the consequence of sheltering, not the verb's meaning.
